messages.subject: Beginner's question: Gaussian random effects model with varying slope and intercept
messages.subject_clean: Beginner's question: Gaussian random effects model with varying slope and intercept
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Firstly thanks for your great work on INLA! I've been using it for some time now and I enjoy it a lot.

My question is: how can I estimate a Gaussian random effects with varying slope and intercept? An example using lme4:

Also, is there any equivalent command for ranef() in lme4, which allows me to check the varying effects' estimates?

Thank you for your attention!

Best,
Danilo

library(lme4)
data(sleepstudy)
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), sleepstudy, REML=FALSE)
summary(m1)
coef(m1)
ranef(m1)
dotplot(ranef(m1, condVar = TRUE))

Thank you so much for your quick reply. I managed to include a random intercept in the model, but I am still not sure if I am adding the random slope correctly (the slopes should be correlated with the group intercepts). My code is presented below.

Sorry the newbie question, I am new to both multilevel modelling and INLA :-)

Best regards,
Danilo

library(lme4)
data(sleepstudy)
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), sleepstudy, REML=FALSE)
summary(m1)

library(INLA)
N <- length(unique(sleepstudy$Subject))
sleepstudy$Subject <- as.numeric(sleepstudy$Subject)
sleepstudy$Subject1 <- as.numeric(sleepstudy$Subject)
m2 <- inla(Reaction ~ 1 + Days + f(Subject, model = "iid2d", n = 2*N) +
             f(Subject1, Days, copy = "Subject"), data = sleepstudy)
summary(m2)

Dear Wim,

You are not specifying the model correctly.

You need to create a new variable combining the factors Region and Month,
and assign an 'iid' model to that variable.

This modified code below works as you expect.

best
ï¿½acu.-

Datax <- within(Data, RegionXMonth <- paste(Region, Month, sep = '.'))

formula = Population_Size ~ Month + f(RegionXMonth, model = 'iid')+Region
model_INLA = inla(formula, data=Datax,
family="gaussian",control.predictor = list(link = 1))

fitted_INLA <- model_INLA$summary.fitted.values$mean

plot(as.numeric(Data$Month), Data$Population_Size)
points(as.numeric(Data$Month), fitted_INLA, col="red")
title('Fit INLA')

messages.subject: Help needed to start building mumodels of multiple multivariate time series
messages.subject_clean: Help needed to start building mumodels of multiple multivariate time series
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I want to end up doing something rather complicated, but I'm struggling at the start.

The full model I'm aiming for is a spatio-temporal model, with a VAR(1) model for a series of sites, and the parameters varying according to a spatial process. For the moment I have 2 simpler questions, which should get me far enough along the road to work out the rest:

1. How do I specify a VAR(1) model? this is a multivariate analogue of an AR(1) process (you can see an example here: http://rspb.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/276/1669/2923.full). I only want to use a bivariate version, so the residual covariance can be modelling with an iid2d term, but how do I introduce the two ar(1) terms, and the two cross-correlation terms?

2. Once I have a VAR(1) model, how do I model the parameters as varying between series (e.g. simply as iid)? I suspect this is straightforward once one understands the thinking behind f(), so I hope it's enough for someone to point me to hte right bit of documentation, and I can take it from there.

Thanks in advance, and have a good weekend!

Bob

VAR(1) models are not implemented in general, only the AR1 (model="ar1")
and AR(p) models (model="ar").

The question is if we can find a way to represent your spesific VAR(1)
model using other means, since this would be a special case. For this it
would be helpful if you could give details of your model so we can check
this out.

Best
H

Hi,
I am attampting to jointly model two point pattern using the spde approach and get the following error message,

t.1<-inla.stack(data=list(y=cbind(pp.1,NA),e=e.1),

                effects=list(i=1:nv,bpp.1=rep(1,nv+nums[1])))

                A=list(A.2,1),tag="pp2",
                effects=list(j=1:nv,bpp.2=rep(1,nv+nums[2])))

I ran the call again with verbose=T the output rather lengthy is below, from what I can see there is a problem with the optimiser trying to find post marginal for theta (i.e. evaluates to NAN), how do I therefore get the optimizer to converge (i.e. do I scale, or set priors?);

Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
A quick and easy thing to check: what is your spatial scale?  INLA runs into problems if the numbers in the mesh are too big (this frequently happens when things come from GIS software or are measured in UTM).  E.g. everything works much better if you scale the earth to have radius 1.

This scaling doesn't effect the inference, it just changes the units and fixes some stability problems.

If it's not that, I'll have a closer look.

Best wishes,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I did this with code below (should be correct) and the above still crashes.

loc<-cbind(wl1$loc[,1]/6378.137,wl1$loc[,2]/6378.137)
bound<-inla.nonconvex.hull(loc)
unitmesh<-inla.mesh.create(boundary=bound,cutoff=100/6378,refine=list(max.edge=500/6378))
Charlotte

On Wednesday, 15 January 2014 13:15:54 UTC, Daniel Simpson wrote:

> A quick and easy thing to check: what is your spatial scale?  INLA runs into problems if the numbers in the mesh are too big (this frequently happens when things come from GIS software or are measured in UTM).  E.g. everything works much better if you scale the earth to have radius 1.
>
> This scaling doesn't effect the inference, it just changes the units and fixes some stability problems.
>
> If it's not that, I'll have a closer look.
>
> Best wishes,
>
> Dan

messages.body_plain:
Have you looked at the resulting mesh?
E.g., is it simply connected?  inla.nonconvex.hull does not guarantee
simple connectedness, so for some clusetered input location sets one
needs to be more careful with the parameters.

Finn

>     A quick and easy thing to check: what is your spatial scale?  INLA
>     runs into problems if the numbers in the mesh are too big (this
>     frequently happens when things come from GIS software or are
>     measured in UTM).  E.g. everything works much better if you scale
>     the earth to have radius 1.
>
>     This scaling doesn't effect the inference, it just changes the units
>     and fixes some stability problems.
>
>     If it's not that, I'll have a closer look.

On 15/01/14 16:00, Charlotte Jones-Todd wrote:
> Hi,
> Your right there's something wrong with the unitmesh. I was initially
> building my mesh from a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame but failed to change
> the CRS to the unit sphere (maybe as I'm missing some simple trick?)
> hence I resorted to the nonconvex.hull method, is there a way to
> circumvent this?

Hard do say without knowing exactly in what way "something is wrong",
but if you're asking how to actually build the mesh on the sphere, it
works like this:

If the meshing function is given 3D coordinates (i.e. in
(x,y,z)-format) it checks if they lie on a sphere, and then builds a
spherical mesh.  So if your original coordinates are in (longitude,
latitude)-format, for example, then you'll need to first transform them
into (x,y,z).  The inla.mesh.map() function can be used for that:

xyz = inla.mesh.map(longlat, projection="longlat", inverse=TRUE)

If you then base a mesh on xyz, all other coordinates must also be
given in xyz-format, e.g. when calling inla.spde.make.A()

/Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
In reference to the problem I posted yesterday, I imagine? the problem is due to numerical overflow in the likelihood, as suggested I have been back and tried a few different (hopefully improved) meshes (which are built from a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object) by ensuring the triangles aren't too diffeent in size etc. I've also set the priors to a few different values in a hope that this would have an effect.
I then reverted back to an original spatial model of mine which just models one point pattern with a spatial effect, an intercept, and two covariates (with the same mesh, wl1<-inla.sp2segment(waleslsoa),
lsmesh4<-inla.mesh.2d(boundary=wl1,cutoff=0.09,max.edge=c(0.5,0.7)) )
 and ran the call with verbose=T, even though this model produces results it still has similar problems in the interim i.e.

.
.

messages.subject: INLA prediction formula
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I used inla to fit my spatio-temporal model and predict future risk. I know how to implement the prediction process, but I am confused about the prediction mechanism. For example, if my Model is
Y(i,t)=Besag(i)+RW1(t)
t=1,2,...9, and I want to predict the values when t=10

Besag(i) part is not time-dependent, so the only difference between years is RW1(t).
And we know RW1(10) follows a normal distribution with mean RW1(9). The best prediction of a normal distribution should be its mean, right?
 In this case RW1(t=10) should be exactly the same as RW1(t=9), so the prediction value of year t=10 should be exactly the fitted value at t=9.

But if we use INLA and implement Y=cbind(Yold, rep(NA, #of_locations)), we got very different values for t=10 than t=9. Could anyone explain to me why and tell me the formula INLA uses for prediction? I am very confused. Thanks a lot

Best
Yuanyuan

Inla computes (approximations of) conditional distributions in a Bayesian framework, so "prediction" is simply a conditional distribution.

messages.body_plain:
I am sorry for not stating my question clearly.
 I have no problem with the running of INLA or the result. But I could't understand the prediction  mechanism.

To simplify, let's us rw1 only model, Poisson family,

library("INLA")
library("MASS")

rw1 = function(time) {
L = matrix(0, time, time)
for(i in 2:time) {
  L[c(i-1, i), i] = c(-1, 1)
 }
Q = L %*% t(L)
return (Q)
}

#Our data is simulated by rw1(50), sigma_t=1
time=50

Mu<-mvrnorm(1, rep(0, time), 1*rw1(time))
Yobs<-rpois(time,exp(Mu))

#Then use the first 49 years as training data, build model, predict the 50th year's data
Ytraining<-c(Yobs[1:(time-1)],NA)

year=c(1:time)
data<-data.frame(y=Ytraining, year=year, ID.year = year)

formula<- y ~ 1+ f(ID.year,model="rw1")
result <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=data,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

Then
result$summary.fitted.values$mean[1:49] should be the fitted mean of Mu[1:49]
And exp(result$summary.fitted.values$mean[50]) should be the predicted mean of Mu[50]
 This is a pretty good prediction, when checked the probability of getting Yobs[50], and it is much different from Mu[49]

What confused me is,  by definition of RW1 distribution, Mu[50] is a normal distribution on Mu[49] only,  and we know the best estimation of a known normal distribution is its mean.
Such that if you predict Mu[50] based on its conditional distribution Normal(Mu[49], sigma),  you should get exactly Mu[49].  Correct me if I am wrong.

So what formula does INLA　use to predict Mu[50]?  If it is by conditional distribution on Mu[49], why isn't the prediction be exactly Mu[49]?

Thanks a lot!

Best
Yuanyuan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA prediction formula
messages.body_plain:
The fitted.values distributions depend on the link function.  You need to specify that the link function should be applied to all predictions, and not only to the ones with observed data (by default it's applied only to non-NA data lines)
Please se the FAQ about predictions on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>.

Also, so you need to be very careful about comparing point estimates; E(exp(x)) is not the same thing as exp(E(x)), for example.  Instead, transform the entire distributions, if needed.

Finn

messages.subject: RAM usage on large models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running INLA on some large models (~80K observations with a latent field of ~110K nodes). I experienced repeated crashes fitting these models. After inspecting the verbose output I did not notice anything meaningful. However, checking the amount of resources used (CPU and RAM) I noticed very large RAM consumption at the end of run (~30 GB), while it was less than 5GB (using 4 threads via num.threads) or less than 2GB (using 1 thread via num.threads) most of job run - see the attached figures (blue is INLA). Is this amount of RAM usage expected for such a kind of a model and data? Is there any way to reduce it, by fitting more coarse approximations?

Thanks!

Regards, Gregor

Hi,

I have tried using num.threads and it did not had any sizeable effect on RAM usage, bit it did have expected effect for the CPU usage as shown on plots in previous e-mail.

I have tried now using the EB integration strategy and this cuts down RAM usage by 10x - see attached plots in this e-mail. This gives me now quite some space to go ahead.

gg

> Yes, the integration part uses memory for each thread; compare with setting num.threads=1.
> The optimization part isn't as parallel.
>
> Inla uses a lot less memory for big models nowadays than a few years ago, but still a lot more than it really needs to use; redesign/implementation likely needed to fix it...
>
> Finn

messages.subject: Linear combination of the predicted probabilities in different Binomial models
messages.subject_clean: Linear combination of the predicted probabilities in different Binomial models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Maybe this question is a little bit strange...

Is it possible to compute a linear combination of the predicted probabilities in different Binomial models?

For example, if I have this 3 models:

n1_i ~ B(p1_i,N1_i)
logit(p1_i)=B0+B1*X1_i

n2_i ~ B(p2_i,N2_i)
logit(p2_i)=B2+B3*X2_i

n3_i ~ B(p3_i,N3_i)
logit(p3_i)=B4+B5*X3_i

I would like to obtain the posterior distribution of this linear combination:

a*p1_i + b*p2_i + c*p3_i where a, b and c are known.

Thank you very much for your help!

Marc

On Thu, 2014-01-30 at 14:35 -0800, Marc Marí-Dell'Olmo wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Maybe this question is a little bit strange...
>
> Is it possible to compute a linear combination of the predicted
> probabilities in different Binomial models?
>
> For example, if I have this 3 models:
>
> n1_i ~ B(p1_i,N1_i)
> logit(p1_i)=B0+B1*X1_i
>
> n2_i ~ B(p2_i,N2_i)
> logit(p2_i)=B2+B3*X2_i
>
> n3_i ~ B(p3_i,N3_i)
> logit(p3_i)=B4+B5*X3_i
>
> I would like to obtain the posterior distribution of this linear
> combination:
>
> a*p1_i + b*p2_i + c*p3_i where a, b and c are known.
>
> Thank you very much for your help!

Marc,

for such problems I think it just easist to use sampling.
inla.posterior.sample will sample from the latent field and the thetas,
and extracting the linear predictors you can just compute samples of the
weighted sum of the p's.

in the case where the model is huuuuge, there is a second option if you
do not need to many of those, that is the define the linear predictors
involved as linear combinations, and then ask inla to compute the
posterior correlation matrix, and then you can approximate their joint
using a Gaussian with these quantities. well, the straight forward
inla.posterior.sample is easier....

Best
H
